methods: adding the two forms of the integral
statement: By using the substitution $x=\\pi-t$, or otherwise, evaluate $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi}\\dfrac{x\\sin x}{1+\\cos^{2}x}\\,dx$.
solution: Let $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi}\\dfrac{x\\sin x}{1+\\cos^{2}x}\\,dx$. Under $x=\\pi-t$, we have $dx=-dt$, $\\sin(\\pi-t)=\\sin t$, $\\cos(\\pi-t)=-\\cos t$, and the limits swap, giving $I=\\int_{0}^{\\pi}\\dfrac{(\\pi-t)\\sin t}{1+\\cos^{2}t}\\,dt=\\pi\\int_{0}^{\\pi}\\dfrac{\\sin t}{1+\\cos^{2}t}\\,dt-I$. Hence $2I=\\pi\\int_{0}^{\\pi}\\dfrac{\\sin t}{1+\\cos^{2}t}\\,dt$. Substitute $u=\\cos t$, $du=-\\sin t\\,dt$: the integral becomes $\\int_{1}^{-1}\\dfrac{-du}{1+u^{2}}=\\int_{-1}^{1}\\dfrac{du}{1+u^{2}}=\\bigl[\\tan^{-1}u\\bigr]_{-1}^{1}=\\dfrac{\\pi}{2}$. Thus $2I=\\pi\\cdot\\dfrac{\\pi}{2}=\\dfrac{\\pi^{2}}{2}$, so $I=\\dfrac{\\pi^{2}}{4}$.
hints: Apply x=π-t to get a second form of I.
Add the two forms to isolate the simpler integral.
Substitute u=cos t to evaluate the remaining integral.
